structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Purpose and regulatory basis: Introduction to BNP Paribas Fortis’ 2024 Sustainability Statements prepared under the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) as transposed into Belgian law, with the aim of enhancing ESG transparency.
- Scope and standards: Report applies cross-cutting and topic-specific ESRS then in force; no industry-specific standards adopted yet, but sector nuances considered to ensure relevance and accuracy.
- Double materiality and material topics: DMA identifies material impacts, risks and opportunities across five topics—climate change, own workforce, consumers and end-users, business conduct (including market integrity and financial security), and cybersecurity.
- Significance and selection of content: Only information deemed material to impacts on people and the environment and to how sustainability affects the bank is included; minor but potentially relevant data may be excluded.
- Methodological approach: Where value-chain data are limited or uncertain, reasonable assumptions and estimates are used, with transparent methods, definitions, limitations, and uncertainties; preference for European regulatory definitions and recognized standards, otherwise internal definitions.
- Forward-looking statements: Contains projections subject to inherent risks and uncertainties; no assurance of achieving targets within set timeframes and no obligation to update unless legally required.
- Climate data uncertainty: Acknowledges evolving methodologies, complex assumptions, and lack of harmonization—especially for Scope 3 financed emissions—leading to measurement uncertainty and potential over/underestimation.
- Third-party information: Some data sourced externally; accuracy and completeness not guaranteed by the bank.
- Structure of the report (table of contents overview):
  - General disclosures: governance; strategy, business model and stakeholders; material IROs.
  - Climate change: strategy; impact, risk and opportunity management; metrics and targets.
  - EU Taxonomy alignment: framework and disclosure obligations, scope, methodology, alignment indicators, limits, and share of aligned assets.
  - Own workforce: strategy; IRO management; metrics and targets.
  - Consumers and end-users: strategy; IRO management; metrics and targets.
  - Business conduct: governance; IRO management; metrics and targets.
  - Additional entity-specific information: market integrity and financial security; cybersecurity.
  - Annexes: supplementary general and climate disclosures, acronyms; plus the accredited statutory auditor’s report.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.heading: 1.a Governance
nodes.start_phrase: The sustainability strategy is integrated at the highest level within the governance bodies.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and reporting: Sustainability statements are prepared on a consolidated basis aligned with the financial consolidation scope, covering BNP Paribas Fortis SA/NV and entities it exclusively controls, and span the full value chain (operational, upstream, downstream).

- Governance for sustainability: ESG is integrated at the highest governance levels. The Board of Directors sets strategy with ESG considerations, supported by four specialized committees (Risk, Audit, Governance & Nomination, Remuneration). The Executive Board/Committee implements and reports on sustainability strategy.

- Board committees’ ESG roles:
  - Risk Committee: incorporates ESG into overall risk strategy and the Risk Appetite Statement; monitors legal/regulatory ESG developments.
  - Audit Committee: oversees CSRD reporting, alignment between sustainability and financial disclosures, and local adaptations of the Group Code of Conduct.
  - Governance & Nomination Committee: evaluates Board skills and ESG knowledge, ensures diversity, reviews integrity policies.
  - Remuneration Committee: integrates ESG objectives into variable pay and applies Group compensation policy.

- Director expertise and training: Board members possess sustainability-related skills; undergo fit-and-proper and suitability assessments; receive induction and ongoing training, including ESG regulation sessions; can access internal/external experts.

- Sustainability management bodies: A Transversal Sustainability Committee coordinates overall ESG strategy and the Sustainability Dashboard, ensuring alignment across five specialized bodies:
  - Sustainable Business Board (business development plan, KPIs).
  - Public Affairs Board (stakeholder dialogue and advocacy).
  - Social Bank Board (societal commitments, support for nonprofits focused on youth inclusion and education).
  - Green Bank Board (decarbonization of infrastructure and operations).
  - ESG Action Plan Board (ESG data management, client ESG strategies and risk oversight).

- Monitoring and internal control: The Board oversees impacts, risks, and opportunities; the Executive Board relies on internal control and supervisory functions. Sustainability reporting controls include a target operating model (data flows, governance, RACI under CSRD), monitoring and validation frameworks, with Finance as second line of defence. The Audit Committee monitors CSRD processes, double materiality, indicators, and related risks.

- Incentives and remuneration: Non-executive directors receive only fixed pay/attendance fees. Executive directors receive variable remuneration tied partly to sustainability objectives via a bonus and a loyalty plan covering economic, social, civic, and environmental targets; 3–5% of total variable pay is linked to climate targets.

- Due diligence: BNP Paribas Group (and thus BNP Paribas Fortis) complies with France’s duty of vigilance law and publishes an annual vigilance plan. The document maps due diligence elements (governance integration, stakeholder dialogue, impact identification, action, monitoring/communication) to relevant sections.

- Strategy, business model, and value chain: A diversified, integrated model across CPBS (retail, professionals, SMEs, corporates, institutions, nonprofits) and CIB (capital markets, M&A, risk management). Strong retail presence (digital, branches, integration of bpost bank) and partnerships to support energy-efficient housing. Corporate clients access specialized financing and transition support via the Sustainable Business Competence Centre and Group expertise (Low Carbon Transition Group, Climate Analytics & Alignment), enabling long-term client transition to low-carbon models.

nodes.title: Strategy, business model and stakeholders
nodes.heading: 1.b Strategy, business model and stakeholders
nodes.start_phrase: BNP Paribas Fortis covers a wide range of activities being part of the Commercial, Personal Banking & Services (CPBS) and the Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB) divisions of BNP Paribas Group:
nodes.summary:
- Legal duty of vigilance and due diligence: BNP Paribas Fortis, as part of BNP Paribas Group, is covered by France’s Law on the duty of vigilance and publishes an annual vigilance plan. The document maps the ESRS-aligned due diligence steps—governance/strategy integration, stakeholder dialogue, impact identification, action, and monitoring/communication—to specific sections of the sustainability statements.

- Strategy, business model, and value chain: The bank operates a diversified, integrated model across CPBS (retail, SME, professional, and institutional banking) and CIB (capital markets, M&A advisory, risk management). It serves individuals and corporates via digital, branch, and partner channels (e.g., bpost bank), and supports client transition with specialized Group teams (SBCC, Low Carbon Transition Group, Climate Analytics and Alignment). Geographic footprint spans EMEA and the Americas; employee counts are provided (Total 35,778; EMEA 35,411; Americas 367). Products/services are presented by ESRS sectors for CPBS and CIB. A value chain view covers upstream (suppliers), internal operations, and downstream commercial activities, including non-bank subsidiaries (Arval, AG Insurance). A double materiality assessment focuses on financing activities within the integrated model.

- Sustainability strategy and objectives: The strategy centers on supporting clients’ transition to a carbon‑neutral, resource‑efficient, inclusive economy, embedded in the Group’s GTS plan and Belgium’s GAS plan. Objectives align to four responsibilities:
  - Economic: financing the transition, ethics, ESG risk integration.
  - Social: people-centric approach via the Group People Strategy (Ethics & Inclusion, Employee Experience, Human Capital).
  - Civic: promoting financial inclusion.
  - Environmental: steering financing/investment toward planetary boundaries and reducing own operational impacts.
  A CSR dashboard reports 2024 results and definitions: €35.9bn sustainable loans; 35% women in Senior Management Positions; 66,165 solidarity hours; 99% of employees completed ≥4 trainings; 3,301 financial inclusion beneficiaries (microStart only, Q3 scope); €16.5bn support to low‑carbon transition; 1.54 tCO2e per FTE. Group 2025 targets are noted for each indicator.

- Implementation priorities in business processes: Five pillars guide delivery—responsible investments, sustainable real estate, sustainable transition of companies, sustainable transport, and social inclusion. Key challenges include incomplete client ESG risk knowledge and limited/variable ESG data quality and methodologies, necessitating estimates.

- Stakeholder interests and dialogue: Clear objectives for stakeholder engagement to understand expectations, inform products/services and strategy, and ensure transparency. Key stakeholders include customers, employees/social partners, investors, suppliers, regulators/public authorities, and civil society/NGOs. Governance frameworks include a Client Interests Protection Policy and a Sustainable Sourcing Charter/Code of Conduct for suppliers. Tailored channels include customer advocacy/NPS and surveys, HR-led employee engagement, supplier relationship management, regulator interactions, and NGO/public affairs dialogues.

- Employee voice, well‑being, and social dialogue: Regular Group pulse surveys (2024 participation: 88% Belgium; 82% overall) and local tools (Team Motivation Barometer, ARPS‑i with IDEWE) inform an action plan on six priorities: pay/benefits transparency; reducing work pressure; psychological safety; disturbance management; empathetic leadership; career opportunities. Social dialogue occurs via the Belgian Workers Council, the Group European Committee (covering 22 countries), and a strengthened 2024 Global Agreement with UNI Global Union and others on rights, equality, well‑being, and freedom of association/collective bargaining. Employee networks (PRIDE, Friends of Africa, MixCity, O2, Ability, Managers in Connection, 35Beaufort) foster inclusion. A whistleblowing system protects the right to speak up.

- Governance integration of stakeholder views: Stakeholder insights are escalated to the Board and Executive Board through sustainable finance governance and the Public Affairs Board; Workers Council consultations enable direct dialogue on ESG strategy and actions.

- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities: A comprehensive ESG risk framework spans onboarding and ongoing KYC/recertification processes. Corporate clients with turnover >€50m undergo an ESG Assessment (questionnaire, controversies, climate factors), documenting ESG maturity, risks, potential impacts, and compliance with sector policies.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 1.c Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase:
The activities of BNP Paribas Fortis’ corporate clients are likely 
to be subject to negative impacts and risks.
nodes.summary:
- Stakeholder engagement and consideration: The bank systematically gathers and integrates views from internal stakeholders (employees, social partners) and external stakeholders (clients, investors, NGOs, regulators) into strategy. HR strategy follows the Group’s People Strategy, reflecting employee expectations on ethics, inclusion, experience, and skills. Company Engagement and Public Affairs maintain regular dialogue with external stakeholders, informing the Sustainability component of the strategic plan and feeding the CSRD-driven double materiality assessment.

- Governance channels for stakeholder input: Stakeholder views on sustainability impacts reach the Executive Board and Board of Directors via sustainable finance governance and the Company Engagement team. The Public Affairs Board presents major sustainability topics raised by investors, clients, and NGOs to the Executive Board twice a year. The Executive Committee regularly consults Worker Council bodies, enabling Q&A on overall and sustainability strategy.

- ESG risk and impact management framework: ESG controls are embedded across relationship onboarding and lifecycle (including KYC recertification). Corporate customers with turnover >€50m undergo systematic ESG assessments (questionnaire, controversy analysis, sector policy compliance). Tools include restricted activities, watch/exclusion lists, sector policies with mandatory ESG criteria, ad hoc CSR analyses, and for project finance, Equator Principles and Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Outcomes range from relationship continuation to enhanced monitoring or termination.

- Double materiality assessment methodology:
  - Structure and scope: Four-step process across the value chain, distinguishing operational vs. commercial activities; addition of two bank-specific topics (Market Integrity & Financial Security, Cybersecurity). Materiality scored 1–5; topics at ≥3 in any of impact/risk/opportunity are material.
  - Impact materiality: Based on 2022–2023 requests from clients, investors, NGOs and 2021 employee survey; refined via internal documentation, reputational considerations, and expert input. Impacts treated as current; positive impacts tied to business opportunities are counted under opportunities to avoid double counting.
  - Financial materiality (risk): Uses the annual Risk ID inventory with forward-looking assessment of risk events, linked to ESG risk drivers, and measured by expected loss against ICAAP thresholds. Includes multiple climate stress-test exercises (RCP/SSP scenarios, real estate flood/acute hazard analyses, ECB 2022 transition stress test) and sector/country ESG tools; future inventories will distinguish short-, medium-, long-term horizons.
  - Opportunity materiality: Anchored in the strategic plan, tied to tracked commitments/KPIs; assessed over the medium term; not climate-specific.

- Governance and controls over IRO: Company Engagement (impacts), RISK (risks), Finance (opportunities) conduct analyses; harmonised and validated by Executive Board/Committee and Board of Directors; integrated with existing internal controls and risk management.

- Results and material topics: A topic is material if stakeholder-perceived negative impacts are significant, risks exceed expected loss thresholds, or opportunities are defined and KPI-tracked in the plan. Annual review foreseen. The matrix identifies environmental, social, and governance topics, with two specific to the bank (Market Integrity & Financial Security, Cybersecurity). Non-banking entities generally align; exception is Arval for pollution impacts in its fleet scope.

- Arval-specific pollution impacts and actions: Identified non-GHG pollution from ICE/hybrid driving (NOx, PM, VOCs, CO), non-renewable electricity for BEV/PHEV charging, brake and tire particulates (including microplastics), and noise. Actions within Arval Beyond/Decarbonisation plan include expanding EV offerings and charging access, sustainable mobility solutions (car sharing, bikes), eco-driving tools/training, vehicle weight management, preventive maintenance, and SMART Repair to reduce waste and chemicals. Governance and implementation handled by Arval across most countries.

- Detailed material IROs by topic (examples):
  - Climate change adaptation/mitigation (commercial activities): Transition risks to client business models creating stranded assets and income decline; indirect financed emissions; reputational risks (greenwashing); opportunities to finance renewables, energy efficiency, and cleaner transport; operational opportunities from reducing own emissions.
  - Own workforce (operational scope): Potential isolated cases of discrimination/exclusion and harassment; HR/legal and human-error risks; opportunities from gender equality, work-life balance, and skills development improving retention, well-being, and costs.
  - Consumers and end-users (commercial activities): Risks of social exclusion from product design and unclear information; privacy/legal risks; opportunities to enhance financial inclusion.
  - Governance: Business conduct risks (corruption/influence peddling); Market Integrity & Financial Security risks (AML/CFT failures with penalties and remediation); Cybersecurity risks (fraudulent data/figures, third-party intrusions and fraudulent payments).

- Integration with overall risk and strategy: ESG risks amplify traditional banking risks and are integrated into risk management and capital adequacy processes. Policies and actions to mitigate impacts/risks and capture opportunities are detailed in thematic chapters (Climate, Own workforce, Consumers and end-users, Business conduct). The strategic plan includes climate and social opportunity indicators.

- Climate change chapter overview:
  - Strategy and transition plan: BNP Paribas Fortis adopts the Group’s transition plan for climate mitigation, focused on financial assets on-balance-sheet and the highest-emitting sectors (e.g., oil & gas, commercial/residential real estate, agriculture). Intermediate reduction targets apply to non-financial corporates within financed emissions scope.
  - Resilience and stress testing: Regular assessment of resilience to physical and transition risks, including ECB/EBA exercises; ICAAP 2050 stress tests affirm model resilience; IFRS 9 reflects climate-related adjustments.
  - Policies and actions: Enhancing counterparty climate profiling, aligning portfolios in high-emitting sectors, reducing operational footprint, and supporting client transition with sustainable products/services.
  - Metrics and targets: Presentation of Group sectoral targets and financed emissions; application of ESRS 1 transitional provision means no absolute GHG reduction target is disclosed at this stage.

structure.title: Climate change
structure.heading: 2 Climate change
structure.start_phrase: BNP Paribas Fortis presents hereafter its strategy, performance and commitments in relation to climate change and in line with the BNP Paribas Group strategy.
structure.summary:
- The document outlines BNP Paribas Fortis’s 2024 climate-change strategy, performance, and commitments, aligned with the BNP Paribas Group.
- It covers:
  - Strategy: a transition plan to align credit portfolios with Paris Agreement–compatible decarbonisation trajectories (section 2.a.1).
  - Climate risk and resilience: regular assessment of physical and transition risks, including ECB/EBA climate stress tests, and analysis of business model resilience (section 2.a.3).
  - Policies: governance and actions to manage material climate impacts, risks, and opportunities (section 2.b.2).
  - Actions: improving understanding of counterparties’ climate profiles, aligning the credit portfolio in high-emitting sectors, reducing operational footprint, and supporting client transition via sustainable products and services.
  - Metrics and targets: disclosure of Group sectoral GHG metrics, BNP Paribas Fortis’s decarbonisation objectives for the most emission-intensive sectors of its credit portfolio, and financed emissions (section 2.c; 2.c.4 for gross GHG).
- Scope and limits:
  - The transition plan applies to financial assets on the BNP Paribas Group and BNP Paribas Fortis balance sheets and focuses on high-emitting sectors.
  - BNP Paribas Fortis’s exposure includes oil & gas, commercial and residential real estate, and agriculture.
  - Intermediate reduction targets apply to financing granted to non-financial corporates in high-emitting sectors within the financed-emissions inventory scope.
- Reporting approach and regulatory context:
  - In the absence of sector-specific standards and amid a stabilising regulatory environment, the bank applies ESRS 1 paragraph 133(a) transitional provision as clarified by EFRAG (FAQ ID1033).
  - As a result, no absolute GHG emission reduction target is disclosed.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 2.a Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: BNP Paribas Fortis has adopted the BNP Paribas Group’s transition plan for climate change mitigation.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Outlines BNP Paribas Fortis’s climate strategy, performance, commitments, and disclosures aligned with the BNP Paribas Group and ESRS guidance, focusing on strategy, climate risk/stress testing, policies, actions, and metrics/targets.

- Transition plan for climate change mitigation:
  - Applies to financial assets on the Group and BNP Paribas Fortis balance sheets, prioritizing highest-emitting sectors (oil & gas, commercial and residential real estate, agriculture).
  - Uses ESRS 1 transitional provision (EFRAG FAQ ID1033); no absolute portfolio GHG-reduction targets disclosed due to data quality/availability (notably Scope 3) and macro uncertainty; relies on medium-term, sector-level intensity targets.
  - Fortis contributes to Group 2025/2030 decarbonization objectives across the most emission-intensive sectors and sets operational intensity targets; residual operational emissions are offset via voluntary carbon credits.

- Sector commitments and portfolio alignment:
  - Progressive exclusions and tightening since 2010 (coal, unconventional oil & gas, Arctic/Amazon); no financing for new oil/gas fields; coal exit by 2030 (EU/OECD) and 2040 (rest of world).
  - Targeted reduction of credit exposure to oil & gas exploration/production by 2030 (−80% oil E&P; −30% gas E&P vs. Sept 2022).
  - Energy financing mix to be at least 90% low‑carbon by 2030; rapid shift already observed.
  - Recognized leadership in sustainable finance (Dealogic 2024).

- Strategy pillars and client support:
  - Align credit portfolios with Paris‑aligned decarbonization trajectories in the most emitting sectors.
  - Support clients’ transition via advisory and financing (e.g., Sustainability‑Linked Loans), and retail green products (energy‑efficient mortgages, lower‑emission vehicle loans).
  - Strengthen internal expertise, tools, processes, and systems; integrate ESG Assessment in corporate credit processes; apply monitoring and exclusion lists under sector policies.

- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities (double materiality):
  - Impact: financed emissions from clients.
  - Risks: transition risks (stranded assets, declining income), reputational risks, and physical climate risks.
  - Opportunities: financing the low‑carbon transition (renewables, energy efficiency, cleaner transport); reducing own operational emissions for cost and reputation benefits.
  - Links presented between material IROs, policies, actions, and targets/metrics.

- Resilience, stress testing, and risk integration:
  - Regular climate scenario analyses via ECB/EBA exercises and annual ICAAP over a 30‑year horizon; results feed provisions, economic capital, and the Risk Appetite Statement.
  - ICAAP 2024 includes three transition scenarios to 2050 (IAM REMIND sub‑2°C, delayed transition, current policies) and physical risk analysis for pluvial/river flood under RCP 8.5 (to 2085), using internal portfolio/ESG data and external macro/climate inputs.
  - Findings: transition could raise cost of risk, especially under disorderly scenarios; physical risks impact collateral values via damage and insurance costs; market risk monitoring adequate; limited climate‑linked operational incidents; teleworking mitigates operational risk; reputational risk managed through scenario assessments.

- Policies:
  - Financing activities governed by sector policies directly linked to climate (Coal‑fired Power, Oil & Gas, Mining, Nuclear), with stakeholder‑informed updates, engagement for monitored clients, and exclusions for non‑compliance.
  - Operational policies prioritize energy efficiency, building optimization, fleet electrification, increased low‑carbon energy use, and Group offsets; employee engagement via EcoCoaches and the Green Company for Employees program; Sustainable Sourcing Charter for suppliers; ISO 14001 certified environmental management in Facility Management; policies on CO2, energy, mobility, paper, and waste.

- Metrics and targets:
  - Disclosure of Group sectoral targets and financed emissions; medium‑term sector objectives for high‑emission sectors; financed emissions inventory scoped per section 2.c with PCAF‑based methods.
  - Operational target example: 2025 direct emissions intensity of 1.85 tCO2e/FTE.

- Governance and compliance:
  - Transition plan contribution endorsed by the BNP Paribas Fortis Executive Board (6 March 2025).
  - Not excluded from EU Paris‑aligned benchmarks per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/1818.

nodes.title: Impact, risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.b Impact, risk and opportunity management
nodes.start_phrase: BNP Paribas Fortis has a range of policies, defined by BNP Paribas Group, that govern its activities and business relationships.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and intent: Extract from BNP Paribas Fortis Sustainability Statements 2024 detailing impact, risk and opportunity management with a focus on climate change mitigation/adaptation policies, actions, governance, operational footprint, transition resources, and sector targets.

- Climate-related policies (financing activities):
  - Group-defined sector policies that directly address climate: Coal-fired power generation, Oil & Gas, Mining, Nuclear Energy.
  - Ongoing updates via stakeholder dialogue (investors, NGOs) and best practices.
  - Monitoring and exclusion lists for non-compliance; engagement for monitored entities; prohibitions for exclusions.

- Operational perimeter policies and practices:
  - Priorities since 2012: energy efficiency in buildings and design, car fleet electrification, increased low‑carbon energy use, voluntary carbon credits for residual emissions.
  - EcoCoaches network (since 2009) to drive employee behavior change.
  - Sustainable Sourcing Charter applied to suppliers; emphasis on supplier ESG.
  - ISO 14001-certified environmental management for Facility Management (Belgium).
  - Policies on CO2, energy, mobility, paper, and waste.

- Governance, scope, and stakeholder interaction (policy summary):
  - Sector policies apply to all BNP Paribas entities/products, overseen by the CEO of BNP Paribas Fortis; made public and shared with clients during KYC and service discussions.
  - Sustainable Sourcing Charter and Environmental Declaration overseen by the COO; engagement includes employees, suppliers, service providers.
  - Internal Travel Policy and Arval employee mobility policy promote lower-impact travel and energy transition across operating countries.

- Actions to implement climate policies:
  - ESG Assessment deployed across corporate clients to integrate ESG risk into credit decisions, monitor controversies, and inform dashboards and credit policies (roll-out from 2021; expanded in 2022+).
  - Portfolio alignment with Paris Agreement using sector reference scenarios (IEA and sector-specific), sector dashboards, client sheets, tooling, and training to steer decarbonisation.
  - Client transition support via sustainable products/services; operational GHG reductions consistent with policy commitments.
  - Arval actions for mobility decarbonisation: fleet electrification, vehicle weight reduction, extended ownership periods.

- Sector portfolio alignment highlights:
  - Oil & gas: end financing for new field developments; phase-out for non-diversified upstream oil; reduce general-purpose lending to upstream. 2024 outcomes: upstream oil exposure cut to €2.2bn and gas to €2.7bn; financed emissions 9.5 MtCO2e (−40% vs 2023, −65% vs Sep-2022).
  - Commercial real estate: intensity 27.7 kgCO2e/m2 (2023), driven by client efficiency and low‑carbon energy mix.
  - Residential real estate (Belgium): large mortgage book (~€60bn); 2023 intensity 58.4 kgCO2e/m2 (−2.1% vs 2022). “My Sustainable Home” supports EPC data collection, policy adaptations (e.g., up to 30-year terms, higher borrowing ratios for efficient assets), and tailored products/services.
  - Agriculture: Group-wide capability building (International Food & Agri hub; Agronomist.pl), Sustainable Agriculture community; levers include biogas/biomethane/digesters, agri-/on-site PV, and sustainable practices (e.g., regenerative agriculture).

- Opportunities linked to the transition:
  - Context: IEA WEO 2024 signals >USD 3T energy investments in 2024, with clean energy dominating; NZE scenario projects >95% low-carbon by 2035.
  - Low-Carbon Transition Group (and MidCaps/SMEs initiative) mobilizes advisory and financing across energy production (renewables and emerging tech), industrial decarbonisation, and sustainable mobility.
  - Retail real estate offering under “My Sustainable Home”: advisor training (>300), EPC capture, preferential financing for efficient homes (HappyNest rent-to-buy solution; Energy Efficient Mortgage Label), low-cost renovation loans, end-to-end renovation support via partners.
  - Mobility solutions via Arval and Personal Finance for EVs and efficient vehicles.

- Operational footprint performance and initiatives (2024):
  - Energy consumption 169 GWh (−8% YoY); electricity is 84% low‑carbon and 74% renewable; renewables supply 52% of total energy (88 GWh).
  - Market-based Scope 1–3 (business travel) emissions: 29,443 tCO2e; significant reduction vs location-based due to electricity sourcing.
  - Real estate: energy monitoring/audits (PLAGE Brussels), portfolio optimization and new HQ with fossil-free heating (STES), PV, and BREEAM Excellent, Passive Building, and WELL Gold certifications; regional masterplan for efficiency and mobility.
  - Employee mobility: telework (up to 50% for most eligible staff), bicycle leasing (>2,000 bikes), better cycling facilities, HQ proximity to public transport (80% PT usage), 95% EV share in 2024 company car orders; awareness campaigns.
  - Sustainable IT: Group-wide methodology and optimization; locally, cloud migration, device recycling with Close The Gap, ESG-integrated procurement, and data strategy to curb duplication.

- Transition resources and capabilities:
  - Group Corporate Engagement, and Fortis Company Engagement & Sustainable Business teams (13 FTE) implement climate policies and stakeholder engagement.
  - Sustainable Business Competence Centre (6 FTE) supports clients and products; partnership with Climact for decarbonisation advisory.
  - Low-Carbon Transition Group (~250 bankers) and LCTM/SMEs accelerate client transitions; Sustainability Academy (Group and Fortis-local) upskills employees.
  - Stress Testing & Financial Simulations team runs ICAAP climate stress tests; Climate Analytics & Alignment team develops sector alignment methodologies and metrics.

- Metrics and targets (credit portfolios):
  - Group commitment to Paris alignment with sectoral targets set from 2022 using IEA NZE 2050 and sector scenarios; baselines between 2020–2022.
  - Oil & Gas: financed emissions target ≤8.2 MtCO2e by 2030 (−70% vs Q3-2022 27.3); upstream exposure targets by 2030: oil ≤€1bn (−80%), gas ≤€3.7bn (−30%).
  - Commercial real estate: reduce intensity from 28.4 kgCO2e/m2 (2022) to 16.7–19.5 by 2030 (−41% to −31%).
  - Residential real estate: Group intensity 35.0 kgCO2e/m2 (2023) vs 35.5 (2022); Belgium 58.4 vs 59.7. (Targets not detailed in this excerpt.)
  - Agriculture identified as a key sector with defined levers; target specifics not included in this section.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 2.c Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: In line with BNP Paribas Group’s strategy, BNP Paribas Fortis has decided to gradually align its credit portfolio with the objectives of the Paris Agreement and contributes, within its scope, to the Group’s objectives.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Details BNP Paribas Fortis’ climate-related metrics, targets and methodologies for credit portfolios, operational footprint, and financed emissions, plus disclosures on European Taxonomy alignment.

- Portfolio alignment strategy:
  - Commitment to align credit portfolios with the Paris Agreement and IEA NZE 2050 scenarios; sector baselines set between 2020–2022.
  - Priority sectors: Oil & Gas, Commercial Real Estate, Residential Real Estate, Agriculture.

- Sector targets and methodologies:
  - Oil & Gas:
    - 2030 targets vs Q3 2022: -80% upstream oil credit exposure (≤ €1bn), -30% upstream gas exposure (≤ €3.7bn), -70% financed emissions (≤ 8.2 MtCO2e; more ambitious than IEA NZE’s -34% sector path).
    - Measurement uses Wood Mackenzie for scopes 1–2 CO2/CH4 and production data for scope 3; IPCC 2006 emission factors and IEA NZE; corporate equity/debt averaged over 3 years.
  - Commercial Real Estate:
    - Scopes 1, 2 and where relevant scope 3 cat.13 (tenant energy); gases include CO2, CH4, N2O, fluorinated gases.
    - Intensity metric kgCO2e/m2 weighted by credit exposure; 2030 target range 16.7–19.5 kgCO2e/m2 (-31% to -41% vs 2022), benchmarked to CRREM V2.02; performance contingent on external factors (national energy mixes, EPC rules).
  - Residential Real Estate:
    - Focus on Scopes 1–2; intensity per m2 (CRREM/PCAF aligned), using EPCs/public data; no quantitative targets set due to heterogeneous energy mixes, regulatory uncertainty, need for coordinated action, and fair transition considerations. Belgium ~32% of CPBS real estate loans.
  - Agriculture:
    - Focus on cultivation/farming (Scopes 1–2). No quantitative target due to sector fragmentation, client data gaps, and immature methodologies/scenarios.

- Opportunities (business activity targets):
  - Group KPI for cumulative support to low‑carbon transition projects (loans, bonds, private placements, advisory, IPOs): €200bn by 2025.
  - Target €40bn credit exposure to low‑carbon energy by 2030 (aiming for 90% of energy production exposure).

- Operational scope management:
  - Data collected annually across ~20 territories (covering ~90% workforce), Oct–Sep reporting period; GHG Protocol basis; includes building energy and business travel (excludes commuting).
  - Target ≤ 1.85 tCO2e/FTE by 2025 (-20.2% vs 2019) achieved.

- 2024 energy consumption and mix:
  - Total energy: 168,603 MWh.
  - Fossil fuels: 68,303 MWh (40.5%).
  - Nuclear: 12,202 MWh (7.2%).
  - Renewables purchased: 87,449 MWh; self‑produced non‑combustible renewables: 649 MWh.
  - Total renewables: 88,098 MWh (52.3%).

- 2024 gross GHG emissions (operational):
  - Total (location‑based): 53,304 tCO2e (-6% vs 2023; -54% vs 2019); 1.54 tCO2e/FTE.
  - Scope 1: 9,059 tCO2e; Scope 2: 29,151 tCO2e (market‑based 5,290 tCO2e); Scope 3 (business travel, cat.6): 15,094 tCO2e.
  - Business travel methodology uses IEA (kWh factors) and DEFRA (km factors).

- 2024 financed emissions (banking book to non‑financial corporates, prudential scope; aligned with EBA/ITS/2022/01):
  - Scope 1 & 2: 15.13 MtCO2e; Scope 3: 6.94 MtCO2e; Total: 22.07 MtCO2e.
  - Inclusions: loans/debt securities/equity to non‑financial corporates on balance sheet.
  - Exclusions (and rationale): insurance asset portfolios (separately reported; pending CSRD standards), trading book (FVTPL), governments & institutions/HQLA and interbank (liquidity/interest rate management, not financing logic), and retail loans (data scarcity, risk linkage, and physical vs transition risk profile).
  - Data/methods: PCAF Part A; attribution via share of financing over enterprise value or total equity+debt; average PCAF data quality score 4.5; 14% coverage with reported S1–2 data; otherwise uses Exiobase sector/geography intensities. Scope 3 estimated only for Oil & Gas and Automotive using portfolio‑observed intensities (limited, low‑quality, <8% coverage).

- Additional mobility leasing disclosure:
  - Arval’s fleet emissions (all scopes across lifecycle) 23.3 MtCO2e in 2024; reported separately in Arval’s CSRD management report.

- Emissions intensity metric:
  - 0.20 MtCO2e per €1bn financed (as of 31 Dec 2024) for the disclosed perimeter.

- Carbon credits and mitigation:
  - Since 2017, annual purchase of voluntary carbon credits to cover prior‑year residual operational emissions (S1, S2, part S3).
  - 2024 purchases cover 2023 emissions; projects include: Kasigau REDD+ in Kenya (Wildlife Works), biodigesters in India (GoodPlanet), forest protection in Guatemala, and improved cookstoves in Peru (Qori Q’oncha); certified by Verra or Gold Standard.

- European Taxonomy alignment disclosures:
  - Explains eligibility vs alignment and minimum safeguards; main indicator for banks is the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), complemented by green ratios for financial guarantees and assets under management.
  - Approach reflects European Commission FAQs (Nov 8, 2024) for DR 2021/2178 interpretation; excludes the conglomerate indicator not in the initial regulation.
  - Scope based on prudential consolidation; measurement on gross carrying amount.
  - GAR numerator includes: exposures to EU companies under NFRD (2024), eligible EU household loans (mortgages, energy renovation loans, car loans since 1 Jan 2022), local administrations for public housing and other specialised financing (use of proceeds known), and repossessed property collateral.

structure.title: Activities aligned with the European Taxonomy
structure.heading: 3 Activities aligned with the European Taxonomy
structure.start_phrase: The European Taxonomy (hereinafter referred to as the Taxonomy) is a system for classifying economic activities according to their contribution to the six1 environmental objectives defined by the European Commission through various Regulations and Delegated Acts published between June 2020 and November 20232.
structure.summary:
- Context: Extract from BNP Paribas Fortis Sustainability Statements 2024 outlining activities aligned with the EU Taxonomy and related disclosures for financial institutions.
- EU Taxonomy framework: Describes the classification system for economic activities contributing to six environmental objectives (climate mitigation, climate adaptation, water/marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention, biodiversity/ecosystems), based on EU Regulations and Delegated Acts (2020–2023).
- Key concepts:
  - Eligibility: Activity is listed in Taxonomy Delegated Regulations due to potential to contribute to an environmental objective.
  - Alignment: Activity makes a substantial contribution, meets all technical screening criteria, does no significant harm to other objectives, and complies with minimum safeguards.
- Main indicator for banks: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) for financing instruments, accompanied by green ratios for financial guarantees and assets under management.
- Methodological stance: Approach draws on European Commission FAQs (8 November 2024) interpreting Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; excludes the FAQs introducing the conglomerate indicator linked to Annex XI.
- Scope for alignment analysis: Indicators calculated on the prudential consolidation perimeter per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178.
- GAR measurement:
  - Based on gross carrying amount (before provisions).
  - Numerator includes Taxonomy-aligned assets across loans/advances, debt securities, equity instruments, and repossessed property collateral.
  - In-scope exposures:
    - European companies subject to the NFRD in 2024.
    - European households for specific loan types: housing loans, energy renovation loans, and car loans originated since 1 January 2022.
    - Local administrations financing public housing and other specialized financing with known use of proceeds.
    - Carrying amount of repossessed property collateral.

nodes.title: Overview of the regulatory framework and disclosure obligations for financial institutions
nodes.heading: 3.a Overview of the regulatory framework and disclosure obligations for financial institutions
nodes.start_phrase: The European Taxonomy (hereinafter referred to as the Taxonomy) is a system for classifying economic activities according to their contribution to the six1 environmental objectives defined by the European Commission through various Regulations and Delegated Acts published between June 2020 and November 20232.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the EU Taxonomy as a classification system for economic activities contributing to six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, water and marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Clarifies two core concepts: eligibility (activity listed in Delegated Regulations) and alignment (activity meeting technical screening criteria, doing no significant harm to other objectives, and complying with minimum safeguards).
- Identifies the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) as the primary alignment indicator for credit institutions, complemented by green ratios for financial guarantees and assets under management.
- Notes the methodological approach relies on the European Commission FAQs of 8 November 2024 interpreting Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, while explicitly excluding the “conglomerate indicator” from Annex XI not foreseen in the original regulation.
- Defines the consolidation scope for disclosures as prudential consolidation per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178.
- States measurement basis for financial assets is gross carrying amount (before provisions).
- Details GAR numerator scope as Taxonomy-aligned assets across loans, advances, debt securities, equity instruments, and repossessed property collateral, specifically including:
  - Exposures to European companies subject to NFRD in 2024.
  - European household exposures in three loan categories: housing loans, energy renovation loans, and car loans granted since 1 January 2022.
  - Exposures to local administrations for public housing financing and other specialised financing with known use of proceeds.
  - Carrying amount of repossessed property collateral.
- Cites the underlying EU Regulation 2020/852 and subsequent Delegated Regulations (2021–2023) establishing criteria and screening requirements.

nodes.title: Scope of financial assets subject to alignment analysis
nodes.heading: 3.b Scope of financial assets subject to alignment analysis
nodes.start_phrase: Each indicator is calculated based on the scope of prudential consolidation as presented in the ‘Risk Management and Capital Adequacy’ chapter of the annual report, in accordance with European Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 of 6 July 2021.
nodes.summary:
- Document context: BNP Paribas Fortis Sustainability Statements 2024, section on activities aligned with the EU Taxonomy.
- Regulatory overview:
  - Explains the EU Taxonomy as a classification system covering six environmental objectives.
  - Distinguishes eligibility (activity listed in delegated acts) from alignment (meets technical screening criteria, does no significant harm, and complies with minimum safeguards).
  - Main banking alignment indicator is the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), complemented by green ratios for financial guarantees and assets under management (AUM).
  - Methodology informed by European Commission FAQs of 8 November 2024 on Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; excludes the later “conglomerate indicator” reference in Annex XI.
- Scope and calculation basis:
  - Indicators calculated on the prudential consolidation scope per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 and measured on gross carrying amounts (pre-provisions).
- GAR methodology:
  - Numerator covers Taxonomy-aligned assets across:
    - European companies subject to the NFRD in 2024.
    - European households for three loan types: housing, energy renovation, and car loans (car loans since 1 Jan 2022).
    - Local administrations for public housing and other specialised financing with known use of proceeds.
    - Repossessed property collateral.
  - Denominator expands to include assets not in the numerator analysis (e.g., interbank deposits, hedging derivatives, non-NFRD European corporates, non-European counterparties, other household loans, cash, tangible/intangible assets, deferred tax assets), creating a structural imbalance.
  - Notes that 44.6% of total assets (gross) are included in the denominator but excluded from numerator analysis, and that exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals (16.1% of assets) are out of scope of the regulation.
  - Introduces a GAR flow indicator measuring the change in aligned assets relative to the change in total covered assets; the same flow approach is applied to other ratios for consistency.
- Off-balance-sheet green ratios:
  - Financial guarantees: numerator limited to guarantees for European NFRD companies; denominator includes all company guarantees, causing structural imbalance; not a representative alignment measure.
  - Assets under management: numerator covers instruments invested in European NFRD companies and real estate; denominator includes all instruments; also not representative due to imbalance.
  - Sovereign/central bank/supranational exposures are excluded from off-balance-sheet indicators.
  - Flow-based indicators for off-balance-sheet items can be calculated for 2024 using the same method as the GAR flow.
- Alignment qualification methodology:
  - Differentiated by counterparty type: NFRD companies, local governments, European households, and investment funds.
  - For NFRD companies with non-allocated financing, alignment shares are sourced from counterparty-reported aligned turnover and CapEx via data providers; applied consistently across GAR, green guarantee ratio, and green AUM ratio.

nodes.title: Methodology for alignment qualification under the European Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 3.c Methodology for alignment qualification under the European Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: The analysis of financial asset eligibility and Taxonomy alignment is based on differentiated approaches depend - ing on the counterparty category: companies subject to the NFRD in 2024, local governments, European households and investment funds.
nodes.summary:
- Explains how the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) denominator includes asset classes not assessed in the numerator—such as interbank deposits, hedging derivatives, exposures to European companies not subject to the NFRD in 2024 and to non-European counterparties, certain household exposures outside GAR loan categories, cash, and other assets—creating a structural imbalance. As 44.6% of total assets are excluded from the numerator but included in the denominator, the GAR is not considered a representative alignment measure.
- Notes that exposures to central governments, central banks and supranational issuers are outside the regulation and account for 16.1% of total balance-sheet assets; these are also excluded from off-balance-sheet indicators.
- Introduces the GAR flow indicator, calculated as the period-over-period change in aligned assets within the change in covered assets, and applies the same flow-based approach to green ratios for financial guarantees and assets under management (AUM) due to a lack of regulatory clarity on off-balance-sheet flows.
- Describes off-balance-sheet green ratios:
  - Financial guarantees: numerator covers guarantees to European companies subject to the NFRD; denominator includes all guarantees, causing a structural imbalance and making the ratio non-representative.
  - Assets under management: numerator covers investments in European NFRD companies and real estate assets; denominator includes all instruments, leading to the same imbalance and non-representativeness. Sovereign-related exposures are excluded.
- Details the European Taxonomy alignment methodology by counterparty:
  - For companies subject to the NFRD where use of funds is not specifically allocated, the bank uses counterparties’ published aligned turnover and CapEx via data providers; this applies to the GAR, green guarantee ratio, and AUM green ratio.
  - Arval’s assets are consolidated for prudential purposes but are not eligible for the GAR numerator; Arval’s aligned turnover/CapEx therefore do not enter BNP Paribas Fortis’ GAR.
  - For financing with known use of funds (companies and local administrations), the European Commission’s 8 November 2024 clarification requires documentary proof for all technical screening criteria; as this is not fully feasible, no such instruments were included in the GAR numerator.
  - For households, full alignment assessment (including DNSH to the other five environmental objectives) is feasible only for housing loans using the bank’s internal physical climate risk system; energy renovation and car loans lack full DNSH evidence and are excluded from the numerator. Thus, only housing loans are included for households.
  - For investment funds under management, the bank has integrated the first alignment indicators published under the SFDR (EU) 2019/2088.
- Presents 31 December 2024 KPIs under Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation:
  - Main KPI (GAR stock): environmentally sustainable assets of EUR 9,780m (turnover) and EUR 9,995m (CapEx); KPI of 3.05% (turnover) and 3.12% (CapEx); coverage over total assets 39.23%; 44.64% of assets excluded from the numerator; 16.13% excluded from the denominator.
  - Additional KPIs: GAR (flow) EUR 9,220m (turnover) and EUR 9,064m (CapEx) with KPIs of -20.20% and -19.87%; financial guarantees EUR 262m and EUR 362m with KPIs of 1.97% and 2.72%; AUM EUR 470m and EUR 516m with KPIs of 3.69% and 4.05%.

nodes.title: Alignment indicator amounts at 31 December 2024
nodes.heading: 3.d Alignment indicator amounts at 31 December 2024
nodes.start_phrase: Summary of key performance indicators (KPI) to be published by credit institutions in accordance with article 8 of the taxonomy regulation
nodes.summary:
- Focus on BNP Paribas Fortis’ EU Taxonomy alignment and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology and results for 2024, including scope, data constraints, and regulatory interpretation.
- Arval: although prudentially consolidated, Arval’s assets are not eligible for the GAR numerator; its aligned shares are disclosed for context (turnover: 13.8% aligned, 97.2% eligible; CapEx: 24.7% aligned, 99.3% eligible) but not reflected in BNP Paribas Fortis’ GAR.
- Use-of-funds financing to companies and local administrations: excluded from the GAR numerator due to the European Commission’s 8 Nov 2024 clarification requiring supporting documents for each technical criterion, which the bank deems operationally infeasible.
- Household lending: only housing loans are included in the GAR numerator; energy renovation and car loans are excluded due to inability to evidence “do no significant harm” (DNSH) criteria across the five other environmental objectives, despite collecting key energy/low-carbon performance data.
- Internal capability: comprehensive DNSH assessment can be applied only to home loans via the bank’s physical climate risk assessment system.
- Investment funds (assets under management): first alignment indicators from SFDR (EU 2019/2088) have been integrated for portfolios under management mandates.
- KPI results as of 31 Dec 2024:
  - GAR stock (turnover-based): 3.05% of covered assets; GAR stock (CapEx-based): 3.12%.
  - Coverage over total assets: 39.23%; assets excluded from GAR numerator: 44.64%; assets excluded from GAR denominator: 16.13%.
  - Additional KPIs: GAR flow (turnover) -20.20%; GAR flow (CapEx) -19.87%; financial guarantees KPIs 1.97% (turnover) and 2.72% (CapEx); assets under management KPIs 3.69% (turnover) and 4.05% (CapEx).
- Composition note: 24.1% of covered assets are eligible but non-aligned (24.0% for climate objectives; 0.1% for other environmental objectives).
- Drivers of negative GAR flow: a denominator reduction from (a) prudential consolidation of Arval and (b) 2024 methodology changes to identify NFRD counterparties; the numerator was only slightly affected and now includes aligned housing loans.
- Disclosures: nine additional tables published for GAR stock related to nuclear energy and fossil gas; further tables for other alignment indicators deemed marginally informative.
- Stated limitations of taxonomy-aligned ratios: methodological imbalances and operational complexity mean they do not fully capture financing of the low‑carbon transition.
- Scope constraints: analysis limited to 2024 NFRD entities, European households, and certain financing to EU local governments; excludes SMEs, non‑EU companies, and project vehicles not under NFRD—even for EU low‑carbon infrastructure—misaligning with the bank’s diversified model.
- Structural ceiling effect: mismatch between numerator scope and total covered assets caps potential ratios at 46.8% in 2024, with lower ceilings for more diversified portfolios.
- Conceptual limits: binary aligned/non‑aligned framework ignores transition trajectories; DNSH and minimum safeguards are hard to evidence due to interpretive and data-access challenges, particularly for retail loans, rendering parts of the bank’s and customers’ transition efforts invisible in GAR.
- Conclusion theme: current regulatory indicators understate the share of assets contributing to EU climate goals and do not fully reflect BNP Paribas Fortis’ transition strategy beyond taxonomy alignment.

nodes.title: Limits of the regulatory ratios for alignment with the European Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 3.e Limits of the regulatory ratios for alignment with the European Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase:
The GAR and other taxonomy-aligned indicators applicable 
to banks face methodological imbalances and operational 
complexity.
nodes.summary:
- Reports BNP Paribas Fortis’ 2024 Green Asset Ratio (GAR), measured via counterparty turnover indicators, at 3.05% of covered assets.
- Details Arval’s contribution: 13.8% aligned share of turnover (97.2% eligible) and 24.7% aligned share of CapEx (99.3% eligible).
- Notes that eligible but non-aligned assets account for 24.1% of covered assets, almost entirely tied to the two climate objectives; only 0.1% relates to other environmental objectives.
- Explains the negative GAR KPI flow (turnover) of (20.2)% as driven by a reduced denominator from Arval’s prudential consolidation and a 2024 methodology change for identifying NFRD counterparties; numerator was little affected and includes newly added aligned housing loans.
- States the bank publishes 13 standard and nine additional GAR stock tables (turnover and CapEx) for nuclear energy and fossil gas; extra disclosures for other alignment indicators deemed of limited added value.
- Describes limitations of EU Taxonomy-based ratios: narrow scope (NFRD entities, EU households, EU local government project finance), exclusion of SMEs, non-European companies, and SPVs; creates a structural ceiling for ratios at 46.8% in 2024, especially for diversified business models.
- Highlights methodological/operational complexity: binary aligned/non-aligned approach overlooks transition trajectories; extensive DNSH and other criteria are hard to interpret and evidence, reducing alignment shares given current data-collection constraints.
- Emphasizes gaps for household energy renovation and car loans where required non-climate data are unavailable, making their climate contributions largely invisible in GARs.
- Concludes that regulatory alignment indicators understate BNP Paribas Fortis’ true contribution and transition efforts; the bank complements them with internal sustainability classification principles inspired by the Taxonomy.
- Introduces an internal ratio focused on key climate performance criteria within eligible assets to better reflect support for EU carbon neutrality: as of 31 December 2024, 11.2% of eligible outstandings for climate objectives are aligned.
- Scope and methodology of the internal ratio: includes NFRD companies (with or without specified use of funds), specialized financing to EU local governments, and EU household loans (mortgages, energy renovation, car loans). Alignment relies on client Taxonomy certificates for defined-use financing, a simplified mitigation-based approach for households, and counterparty KPIs for undefined-use financing.
- Presents figures (Table 16): total eligible assets €86,974m; aligned €9,780m (11.2%). Within this, NFRD counterparties €5,334m eligible with €585m aligned (11.0%); households €81,640m eligible with €9,195m aligned (11.3%).

nodes.title: Share of assets aligned with climate performance criteria in eligible assets
nodes.heading: 3.f Share of assets aligned with climate performance criteria in eligible assets
nodes.start_phrase: The internal ratio developed by BNP Paribas Fortis emanating from assets aligned with key climate performance criteria within eligible assets provides a clearer view of how the bank’s financing supports the EU’s carbon neutrality objectives.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on EU Taxonomy alignment and internal climate performance metrics for BNP Paribas Fortis’ financing, alongside an overview of own workforce strategy, policies, actions, and metrics.
- Notes limitations of the EU Taxonomy (criteria not fully developed for non-EU activities); bank uses internal sustainability classification principles inspired by the Taxonomy.
- Introduces an internal ratio showing assets aligned with key climate performance criteria within eligible assets to reflect support for EU carbon neutrality.
- As of 31 December 2024, 11.2% of eligible outstandings for climate objectives are aligned: €9,780m aligned out of €86,974m eligible; 11.0% alignment for NFRD counterparties (€585m/€5,334m) and 11.3% for households (€9,195m/€81,640m).
- Scope covers EU NFRD companies (regardless of use-of-funds), specialised financing to European local governments, and EU household loans (mortgages, energy renovation, car loans).
- Alignment methodology uses a simplified approach focused on technical climate performance criteria:
  - Defined use-of-funds corporate financing: client-provided Taxonomy alignment certificate specifying aligned share and objective.
  - Household loans: simplified assessment based on substantial contribution to climate change mitigation criteria.
  - Undefined use-of-funds corporate financing: assessment via counterparties’ published KPIs per earlier-described methodology.
- Positions the internal ratio as more reflective than the GAR of the bank’s strategy to finance low-carbon energy and support low-carbon housing, renovation, and mobility in Europe; links to broader portfolio alignment strategy in the Climate Change chapter.
- Disclosures: generic tables are in the annex; in addition to 13 generic tables, 9 complementary tables to the GAR (turnover and CapEx bases) cover financing related to fossil fuels and nuclear energy; other secondary alignment indicators deemed marginally useful are not expanded.
- Own workforce section (circa 35,000 staff, 98% permanent; includes some temporary agency workers) follows BNP Paribas Group’s People Strategy centered on ethics and inclusion, employee experience, and human capital, adapted locally.
- Presents strategy, policies, actions, targets, and metrics for workforce management, informed by a double materiality assessment and stakeholder feedback (employees, NGOs, customers, investors).
- Actions include promoting inclusion; preventing discrimination, harassment, and violence; ensuring social protection; preventing psychosocial risks; advancing professional equality; supporting civil society; and developing skills.
- Targets include commitments from the Group’s Global Agreement and CSR dashboard; metrics cover employment conditions, working hours, pay, social dialogue, wellbeing, work-life balance, health and safety, and equal treatment (including training, disability, diversity, anti-harassment measures).
- Risk and impact assessment indicates varying risk by geography and role; identified negative impacts primarily concern discrimination, inequality, exclusion, and isolated cases of workplace violence/harassment; these do not stem directly from strategy, but the bank remains vigilant to stakeholder concerns.

structure.title: Own workforce
structure.heading: 4 Own workforce
structure.start_phrase:
The own workforce relates to BNP Paribas Fortis’ employees, of 
whom there were slightly more than 35,000 as at 31 December 
2024, mostly on permanent contracts (98%).
structure.summary:
- Section outlines BNP Paribas Fortis’ “Own workforce” within its 2024 Sustainability Statements, covering slightly over 35,000 employees (98% permanent) plus temporary agency staff.
- HR approach aligns with BNP Paribas Group policies, adapted locally, and is driven by a People Strategy focused on ethics and inclusion, employee experience, and human capital.
- A double materiality assessment identifies workforce-related material impacts, risks, and opportunities, integrating stakeholder feedback (employees, NGOs, customers, investors) and internal risk analyses across business lines and geographies.
- Policies and remedial actions target inclusive culture, prevention of discrimination, harassment and workplace violence, social protection, psychosocial risk prevention, professional equality, civic engagement, and skills development.
- Targets derive from the Group’s Global Agreement and the CSR dashboard; metrics span workforce composition and flows, employment conditions, working hours, fair pay, social dialogue, wellbeing, work-life balance, health and safety, equal treatment, training and upskilling, disability inclusion, diversity, and anti-violence/harassment measures.
- As a responsible employer, the bank commits to respecting labor rights and providing a healthy, fair working environment, recognizing varying risk levels by geography and role.
- Identified material negative impacts include discrimination, inequality, exclusion, and isolated cases of violence and harassment; these do not stem directly from the strategy, but the bank remains vigilant to stakeholder interests.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 4.a Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: As a responsible employer, BNP Paribas Fortis ensures that the labour rights of its workers, including employees and temporary workers, are respected.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Focus on BNP Paribas Fortis’ own workforce (>35,000 employees as of 31 Dec 2024, 98% on permanent contracts), also including certain temporary agency workers.
- Governance and strategy: Aligns with BNP Paribas Group’s HR strategy; “People Strategy” centers on ethics and inclusion, employee experience, and human capital. A double materiality assessment informed by stakeholders identifies workforce-related impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Material impacts: Risks of discrimination, inequality, exclusion, and occasional workplace violence/harassment; potential gaps in social protection in some countries of operation; exposure to incivility from clients/external parties.
- Material risks: Psychosocial risks linked to changing work patterns and remote work (stress, burnout, sedentary risks), and HR legal risks (discrimination/harassment or contract disputes) with potential financial impact.
- Opportunities: Advancing gender diversity (especially in senior management and IT), improving work-life balance through solidarity/volunteering hours, and strengthening skills development and internal mobility (4,872 role transfers in 2024), enhancing engagement, retention, and performance while reducing recruitment costs.
- Policies: Code of Conduct, Global Agreement, Respect for Persons policy, Diversity governance, Compensation/Remuneration and External Recruitment policies, People & Property Policy, Professional Path Policy, and the European Agreement on the Prevention of Stress at Work. Policies apply to all staff; no specific “vulnerable” groups identified.
- Actions: Inclusion initiatives; confidential whistleblowing and remedial measures for discrimination/harassment; social protection and assistance via We Care and employee assistance programs; stress measurement; mental health and managerial training; Women in IT and awareness campaigns; #1MillionHours2Help volunteering; skills management tools, Career Days, About Me platform, continuous development and mobility initiatives; active social dialogue.
- Metrics and monitoring: Workforce and non-employee characteristics; diversity and remuneration data; adequate wage; collective bargaining/social dialogue; training and skills development; work-life balance; health and safety; social protection; severe human rights cases/complaints/incidents; alerts and sanctions related to respect for persons.
- Targets: 40% women in Senior Management Positions by 2025; women in IT at 31% by 2026 and 35% by 2030; 1 million solidarity hours over a rolling two-year period at Group level; 90% of employees to complete at least four trainings annually; 100% coverage with listening and psychological support mechanisms; ongoing monitoring of respect-for-persons alerts and related sanctions.
- Overall aim: Ensure respect for human rights, a healthy, safe, inclusive, and equitable workplace, mitigating risks and leveraging opportunities to support employee well-being and organizational performance.

nodes.title: Impacts, risks and opportunities management
nodes.heading: 4.b Impacts, risks and opportunities management
nodes.start_phrase: Through its policies, BNP Paribas Fortis places particular emphasis on human rights, health and safety at work and diversity, equality and inclusion.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: BNP Paribas Fortis Sustainability Statements 2024 sections on own workforce (impacts, risks, opportunities, actions, metrics, and targets).
- Policy framework: Comprehensive suite covering Code of Conduct, security and crisis management, deployment of the BNP Paribas Group Global Agreement, respect for persons (including a single whistleblowing system), sanctions for misconduct, Diversity & Inclusion governance, external recruitment, professional path/career management, and remuneration (including significant risk takers).
- Human rights and ethics: Alignment with UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles, International Bill of Human Rights, and ILO conventions; low modern slavery risk; supplier adherence via the Sustainable Sourcing Charter and audit rights; accessible remediation and whistleblowing channels for employees and value-chain workers.
- Health and safety: Group-approved framework for security, safety, business continuity, and crisis management; site compliance with local regulations; actual risks assessed as low, with main focus on psychosocial and sedentary risks.
- Diversity, equality, inclusion (DEI): Strong commitments across gender equality, LGBTQ+ inclusion, origins/multiculturalism, age, and disability; fair and bias-aware HR processes (recruitment, appraisal, pay, careers); mandatory conduct and DEI training; structured procedures to prevent, investigate, and remediate discrimination/harassment with protections for whistleblowers.
- Social dialogue and engagement: Ongoing employee and representative engagement; renewed 2024 Global Agreement with UNI Global Union (four-year term) covering seven themes including social dialogue and whistleblowing.
- Whistleblowing and remediation: Group-wide, secure, confidential platform open to employees and external parties; clear investigation, corrective, and disciplinary pathways; anti-retaliation protections; multi-level controls and regular executive/board reporting; high employee awareness (93% know reporting channels).
- Inclusion and prevention actions:
  - Inclusion Days: large-scale awareness events across multiple inclusion topics with broad participation.
  - Preventing discrimination/harassment: mandatory training, awareness, reporting reinforcement, and performance objectives linked to conduct.
  - Social protection: minimum global benefits (healthcare, disability/incapacity/death insurance), paid maternity (≥14 weeks) and paternity (≥6 days) leave; childcare leave enhancements in 2024 agreement.
  - We Care program: mental health support (EAP and crisis support), stress prevention training, forthcoming voluntary health assessments, and support for long-term illness.

structure.summary: The excerpt outlines the 2024 Sustainability Statements chapter on Consumers and End-Users at BNP Paribas Fortis. It defines the scope as direct individual customers and indirect beneficiaries reached via microfinance institutions, and structures the chapter around four themes: data privacy protection; transparent, clear and non-misleading information; customer satisfaction; and social inclusion. The framework covers Strategy (double materiality assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities), Policies (Code of Conduct, Personal Data Protection Policy, Protection of Customer Interests Policy), Actions (dialogue and complaints channels, data protection governance and procedures, use of the Net Promoter System, targeted financial inclusion offers, and employee training), and Metrics/Targets (notably the BNP Paribas Group goal to serve six million financial-inclusion beneficiaries by 2025, tracked via the CSR dashboard). nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 5.a Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: The double materiality assessment revealed several material impacts, risks and opportunities affecting BNP Paribas Fortis’ consumers and end-users.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and audience: Focuses on consumers and end-users of BNP Paribas Fortis—direct individual customers and indirect beneficiaries via microfinance partners.
- Thematic pillars: 
  1) Data privacy protection; 
  2) Transparent, clear, non-misleading information; 
  3) Customer satisfaction; 
  4) Social inclusion.
- Strategy and double materiality:
  - Material impacts: financial difficulties from inadequate information; customer dissatisfaction from operational/commercial issues; barriers to access affecting social inclusion.
  - Material risks: legal and reputational exposure from personal data breaches and GDPR non-compliance.
  - Material opportunities: products and services advancing financial inclusion and, by extension, social inclusion.
  - Interaction with strategy: Negative impacts and risks are unintended (design/delivery or compliance failures), while inclusion opportunities are strategic priorities; social inclusion is one of five Group priorities.
- Policies and governance:
  - Code of Conduct (bank-wide conduct rules).
  - Group Personal Data Protection Policy (locally adapted; DPO/CRO oversight; customer-facing Notice of Information).
  - Policy on Protection of Customer Interests (rules across the full customer lifecycle).
  - Ongoing and periodic internal controls; personal data policy monitored by Data Office and RISK.
  - Alignment with international standards (e.g., UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights); GDPR compliance embedded.
  - Whistleblowing system available to internal and external stakeholders; retaliation protections strengthened in 2023 (EU Directive 2019/1937).
- Actions and management:
  - Customer dialogue and complaint channels; rules for informing and responding to customers.
  - Clear, transparent, non-misleading information practices, including formal drafting guidelines for commercial documents.
  - Data protection risk management process and dedicated governance.
  - Net Promoter System to drive customer satisfaction and continuous improvement.
  - Financial inclusion initiatives and offers (e.g., microStart, Nickel, DigitAll).
  - Cross-cutting employee training and continuous improvement processes.
- Metrics and targets:
  - KPI: number of beneficiaries of products/services promoting financial inclusion (reported in the CSR dashboard).
  - Group target: six million financial-inclusion beneficiaries by 2025, with BNP Paribas Fortis contributing.
- Linkage overview:
  - Impacts (lack of info, dissatisfaction, ineligibility) tied to Code of Conduct and Customer Interests policy; addressed via training, transparent information, complaint handling, NPS, and inclusion offers.
  - Risks (data loss/theft) tied to Code of Conduct and Personal Data Protection policy; addressed through training, risk processes, governance, dialogue, and continuous improvement.
  - Opportunities (financial inclusion) advanced via inclusion offers and tracked by the beneficiaries KPI.

nodes.start_phrase: To manage the material impacts of its products and services on consumers and end-users, as well as the material risks and opportunities associated with them, BNP Paribas Fortis has several policies which are summarised in the table below.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: This section of the BNP Paribas Fortis Sustainability Statements details how the bank manages material impacts, risks, and opportunities related to consumers and end-users, covering governance policies, engagement and remediation processes, data privacy, customer satisfaction, social inclusion initiatives, effectiveness, and targets.

- Consumer and end-user policies and governance:
  - Code of Conduct, Group Personal Data Protection Policy (locally adapted), and Policy on Protection of Client Interests govern all interactions with consumers and end-users.
  - Oversight by the Board of Directors, CRO, Data Office, RISK, Compliance, and internal audit; policies aligned with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
  - Whistleblowing system accessible to internal and external stakeholders; strengthened anti-retaliation protections in line with EU Directive 2019/1937.
  - Commitment to privacy aligned with GDPR; BNP Paribas Fortis does not sell customers’ personal data.

- Customer engagement and transparency:
  - Principles for transparent, fair, clear, and non-misleading information before and throughout the product lifecycle; adherence to stricter local rules where applicable.
  - Employee training on customer interest protection and internal controls to ensure compliance.

- Customer satisfaction measurement and outcomes:
  - Continuous “Advocacy” program using multi-channel NPS benchmarks, relationship and transactional surveys, CES, and monitoring of spontaneous feedback (complaints, social media).
  - 2024 results highlight: Retail NPS improved (boosted by former bpost bank customers), Fintro maintains leading NPS; strong positions across B2B segments (market-average to leader status by segment); Priority Banking NPS up; Private Banking ranked #1 in Belgium for the fourth year; Wealth Management with very high recommendation levels. Relationship management quality is a key driver.

- Complaints handling and remediation:
  - Clear, free complaint process with SLAs: acknowledgement within five working days and response within one month; customers kept informed of progress.
  - Independent mediation/ombudsman available; processes monitored by Compliance.
  - Structured root-cause analysis and continuous improvement; regular reporting to COO and Board/Executive Committee.
  - Individual remediation via follow-up calls within five days to surveyed customers; systemic issues escalated to central teams; supported by Customer Feedback Management tools and dashboards.
  - A dedicated Customer and Employee Knowledge Centre governs NPS standards, aggregates feedback, conducts analyses, drives prioritisation with operations, and brings the customer voice into decision-making.

- Data privacy protection:
  - Risk-based approach to personal data processing with organisational and technical controls per GDPR Article 32 (pseudonymisation, encryption, confidentiality/integrity/availability/resilience, recovery capabilities).
  - Governance via Chief Data Officers (first line) and Data Protection Officers (second line), supported by Legal experts; third line verifies application and effectiveness.
  - GDPR-aligned customer dialogue: timely breach notifications; clear channels for requests/complaints detailed in the privacy notice; subcontractors must support responses; confidential and secure handling.
  - Ongoing monitoring, audits, and supervisory oversight; lessons from incidents and interactions feed continuous improvement.

- Actions on transparency and anti-misleading practices:
  - Formalised guidelines for drafting commercial materials and best practices to avoid greenwashing.
  - Clear communication of complaint and mediation protocols online and at public reception sites.

- Training and culture:
  - Mandatory “Conduct Journey” program (with whistleblowing and DE&I modules), personal data protection training, cybersecurity awareness.
  - Sustainability Academy (Group and local BNP Paribas Fortis version) on sustainable finance, social and financial inclusion.

- Social inclusion and financial inclusion initiatives:
  - Microfinance: Financing via microStart in Belgium (co-founded by BNP Paribas Fortis), integrated into the bank’s offer; >600 employees trained to support referrals and access.
  - Nickel: Accessible current accounts and payment cards without conditions to enable participation in economic life.
  - DigitAll: Bank-initiated coalition (now a Belgian non-profit) to drive digital inclusion, with a broad ecosystem and a widely signed Charter for Digital Inclusion.
  - Impact Entrepreneurs: Tailored credit analysis incorporating social/environmental impact; €42m in new loans in 2024; participation in Trividend to expand the ecosystem.

- Effectiveness and continuous improvement:
  - Regular assessment of actions across data privacy, transparency, customer satisfaction, and social inclusion; adherence to response-time rules; GDPR-aligned risk management prevents negative impacts and supports inclusion (e.g., through encryption/pseudonymisation).
  - Code of Conduct underpins high ethical standards in data protection.

- Metrics and targets:
  - Group target: 6 million beneficiaries of financial inclusion products/services by 2025 (CSR dashboard), to which the bank contributes.
  - microStart contribution since 2011: €66m in loans, 7,621 loans supporting 5,653 projects, >8,000 jobs; Q3 2024: 3,301 beneficiaries; in 2024: 466 loans totaling €4.8m and 1,137 micro-entrepreneurs supported.

- Risk management focus areas:
  - Anti-corruption, AML/CTF: comprehensive detection systems, mandatory training, evolving digital tools.

- Whistleblowing system:
