  - Market Integrity Programme aligned with regulations and good practices (incl. FSMA), built on policies/procedures, IT tools, specialised teams, independent controls/audit, and ongoing training.
  - Two core activities:
    - Managing inside information and preventing conflicts of interest: permanent record‑keeping of inside information/holders, information barriers and activity segregation (IB, proprietary trading, asset management), policies on sensitive info, market surveys, index contributions, and data confidentiality; detection and prevention processes for conflicts of interest (incl. issuer/customer lists).
    - Monitoring transactions and communications to protect market transparency: market abuse prevention/detection/reporting (insider dealing, manipulation, false information) across brokerage and own-account/market-making; FSMA reporting; supervision of orders/transactions; compliance with pre/post-trade transparency and post-trade reporting; monitoring of oral/electronic communications; threshold crossing and short position reporting.

- Financial security (7.a.2):
  - Firm compliance with AML/CFT and international sanctions; implementation of a Group-designed, Belgium-adapted, risk-based Financial Security Programme with significant human/technical resources and the same five pillars (policies, tools, specialised teams, independent controls/audit, training).
  - Three main activities:
    - Know Your Customer (KYC): identification of customers/beneficial owners/agents, analysis of activity/nexus/purpose of relationship; enhanced due diligence for high-risk clients and PEPs; similar checks for suppliers and partners; supports AML/CFT, sanctions compliance, anti-corruption, tax compliance, customer protection, CSR, and market integrity.
    - Compliance with sanctions/embargoes (EU, France, Belgium, US, others): periodic screening of customer databases; screening of international/domestic transactions; continuous list updates; investigations of alerts; authority reporting; staff training and independent controls.
    - Combating money laundering and terrorism financing: IT monitoring and staff vigilance to detect/report suspicious activity (e.g., corruption, tax crime, drug trafficking, organised crime, misappropriation; TF from legal/illegal sources); defined procedures for alert handling, reporting, and follow-up.
  - Geographic risk integration: Group country/region risk assessment applied by BNP Paribas Fortis (with local specifics) may trigger avoidance/termination of relationships or refusal of transactions/services.

- Cybersecurity (7.b):
  - General context (7.b.1): ICT is core to operational resilience; exposure to evolving, sophisticated cyber threats (including ransomware) affecting own and third‑party services; potential impacts include service disruption, data breaches, financial loss, reputational harm, and regulatory fines; regulators view cyber risk as systemic and demand stronger resilience and controls.
  - Governance (7.b.2): Executive Committee oversight; Information Security Steering Committee (ISSC) tracks programme rollout, priorities, and budget; IT Risk Management Committee (ITRMC) addresses cyber, IT strategy, and operational resilience risks; “three lines of defence” model—1st line (CIO/IT/functions manage cyber risk), 2nd line (RISK Function check & challenge), 3rd line (Inspection Générale audits).
  - Policies and responsibilities (7.b.3): Bank-wide cybersecurity system based on a reference framework and Group strategy “Cyber Trust 25”; policies/standards/norms aligned with industry best practices to ensure consistent processes and controls across the entity.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity
nodes.heading: 7.b Cybersecurity
nodes.start_phrase: In the ever-changing landscape of the global financial industry, BNP Paribas Fortis recognises the central role of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) in maintaining opera - tional resilience.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Cybersecurity at BNP Paribas Fortis, outlining risk context, governance, policies, actions, targets, and metrics, followed by annex disclosures on reporting scope and estimation uncertainties under CSRD.
- Cyber risk context: The bank faces evolving cyber threats (intrusions, ransomware, data theft, service disruption) amplified by interconnected operations, rapid tech change, and third-party reliance. Failures could cause financial loss, reputational damage, and regulatory fines. Regulators view cybercrime as a systemic financial-sector risk and demand stronger resilience.
- Governance: Oversight by the Executive Committee. The Information Security Steering Committee monitors the cybersecurity programme, priorities, and budget; the IT Risk Management Committee addresses cyber risks, IT strategy implementation, and operational resilience. Governance follows the three lines of defense: first line (CIOs/IT functions manage cybersecurity), second line (RISK function’s independent challenge), third line (Inspection Générale audits).
- Policies and responsibilities: A mandatory Group Cybersecurity Reference Framework (policies, standards, norms) aligned with best practices standardizes controls across entities; local add-ons may address specific risks. Group strategy “Cyber Trust 25” has five pillars: responsibility to customers/regulators, market leadership/talent, accelerated transformation/innovation, positive work environment tied to CSR, and zero digital waste aligned to business risk. The BNP Paribas Fortis ISSO defines vision/strategy, integrates cyber/ICT risk into projects, and leads the cybersecurity programme. Certain consolidated entities (Arval, BGL BNP Paribas, TEB) run similar local governance and report to the Group CISO.
- Actions: Requirements from the Cybersecurity Framework are reviewed for scope/applicability/timelines; risk-based action plans with milestones, responsibilities, and resource allocation are executed. Budgets are adjusted as needed. Cyber Trust 25 ambitions translate into initiatives and deliverables, adaptable to evolving threats.
- Targets: Each requirement has a due date. Progress is tracked via a risk-based maturity model with objectives set in a cybersecurity matrix. Cyber Trust 25 initiatives have targeted, quantified action plans and goals.
- Metrics: Annual campaigns assess compliance and objective achievement, with results reported to management. Progress on Cyber Trust 25 is monitored in dedicated committees using indicator dashboards. Self-assessments leverage generic ICT control libraries to test governance, risk, and cybersecurity controls, identify gaps, and define remediation.
- Annex highlights:
  - Reporting scope: Certain EU subsidiaries meeting CSRD size thresholds but not listed (BNPP Lease Group France; BGL BNP Paribas, Luxembourg) are exempt under Articles 19a(9) and 29a(8) and are covered by BNP Paribas Fortis’ consolidated sustainability statements.
  - Specific circumstances disclosures: Clarifies deviations in time horizons, use of estimated value chain data (e.g., climate stress tests; Scope 3 categories 15—investments—and 6—business travel; sector targets/baselines), bases of preparation, accuracy levels, and planned improvements. Addresses sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty, including assumptions and judgements applied.

nodes.summary:
This section presents BNP Paribas Fortis’ Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures for 31 December 2024, focused on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and related KPIs for both stock and flow, measured on turnover and CapEx bases.

Key headline KPIs and coverage:
- GAR (stock): EUR 9.78bn taxonomy-aligned assets on a turnover basis (KPI 3.05%) and EUR 9.995bn on a CapEx basis (KPI 3.11).
- GAR (flow): -20.20% (turnover) and -19.87% (CapEx).
- Denominator coverage: 39.23% of total assets; assets excluded from the numerator 44.64%; assets excluded from the denominator 16.13%.
- Off-balance sheet KPIs: Financial guarantees KPI 1.97% (turnover) and 2.72% (CapEx); Assets under management KPI 3.69% (turnover) and 4.05% (CapEx).

Scope, composition and exclusions:
- Detailed mapping of assets covered in both numerator and denominator (EUR 150.2bn), assets excluded from numerator but included in denominator (EUR 170.9bn; e.g., SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD, non‑EU counterparties, derivatives, interbank on demand, cash and other assets), and assets not covered by GAR (EUR 61.8bn; central governments/supranationals, central banks, trading book). Total assets: EUR 382.8bn; total GAR assets: EUR 321.1bn.
- Breakdowns by counterparty and instrument: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial corporates, households (notably residential mortgages and renovation loans), and local governments; and by loans, debt securities, and equity.
- Parallel disclosures for off-balance sheet exposures to undertakings subject to NFRD (financial guarantees and assets under management), with eligible and aligned amounts on both turnover and CapEx bases.

Environmental objectives and activity types:
- Comprehensive allocation across the six EU Taxonomy environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
- Identification of activity categories contributing to alignment: use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.

Sector detail and KPI ratios:
- Granular NACE sector breakdowns (e.g., electricity generation and distribution, manufacturing subsectors, construction, transportation and storage, real estate), separating undertakings subject to NFRD from SMEs/other NFCs.
- Percentage KPI tables for stocks and flows show the proportion of total covered assets that are taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned by asset class and counterparty, including the contribution of households (notably residential mortgages) to eligible and aligned volumes.
